title: Grand jury and administrative subpoenas — basic subscriber information
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. A subpoena compels production of basic subscriber records: name, address, payment method, session times and durations, and temporarily assigned network addresses. Subpoenas do not authorize disclosure of communications content or CSLI. They are the lowest rung of the Stored Communications Act process ladder and are issued without prior judicial approval. title: 2703(d) court orders — specific and articulable facts
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. A court order under 18 U.S.C. 2703(d) requires the government to show specific and articulable facts giving reasonable grounds to believe the records are relevant and material to an ongoing criminal investigation. After Carpenter, 2703(d) orders remain available for non-content records and for CSLI periods below the seven-day warrant threshold, subject to evolving case law on real-time and short-term location data. title: Search warrants under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41 — the Carpenter standard
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Post-Carpenter, obtaining seven or more days of historical CSLI requires a search warrant supported by probable cause, with particularity describing the records sought. Rule 41 warrants are issued by a neutral magistrate, may include delayed notice under 2705, and are the constitutionally required process for the "exhaustive chronicle" of location information. title: Pen register and trap-and-trace orders — prospective signaling data
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Under 18 U.S.C. 3121-3127, the government may obtain a court order for prospective collection of non-content dialing, routing, addressing, and signaling information on certification of relevance to an ongoing investigation. Orders run up to 60 days with extensions. Courts increasingly scrutinize whether prospective location signaling triggers Carpenter warrant requirements. title: Title III wiretap orders — real-time content interception
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Real-time interception of communications content requires a Title III order under 18 U.S.C. 2518: probable cause that specific communications concerning the offense will be obtained, plus a necessity showing. Location information that is content-adjacent or that constitutes a search under Carpenter is handled under Fourth Amendment warrant standards rather than Title III. title: Exigent circumstances and emergency disclosure
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. When there is an imminent danger of death or serious physical injury, providers may voluntarily disclose location information in an emergency under 18 U.S.C. 2702, and officers may act without a warrant under the exigent-circumstances doctrine. Emergency disclosures are documented, subject to after-the-fact review, and carriers publish dedicated emergency-request procedures. title: Consent — voluntary disclosure by the user
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. A subscriber or user may voluntarily consent to disclosure of their own location records, and one party's consent can authorize certain disclosures under 2702. Consent must be knowing and voluntary; coerced or uninformed consent is invalid. Consent-based acquisition is common in missing-person and victim-assistance contexts. title: Preservation requests — 90-day hold under 2703(f)
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Before formal process issues, investigators may send a 2703(f) preservation request requiring the provider to retain specified records for 90 days, renewable once. Preservation is the standard opening move in CSLI investigations: it freezes the retention clock while subpoenas, orders, or warrants are prepared, and creates no disclosure obligation by itself.
